body.heading: The rainbow recipe
paragraphs: A rainbow needs two ingredients at the same time: rain falling and sun shining. That is why rainbows often appear when a shower is ending and the sun peeks out.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really many colours mixed together. Each raindrop bends the light and separates the colours, like a tiny glass prism.

body.heading: Where to stand
paragraphs: To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you. Turn your back to the sun — never look at the sun itself — and search the sky over the rain.
Rainbows are often easiest to spot in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low. At lunchtime the sun is too high for most rainbows.

body.heading: Colours in order
paragraphs: A rainbow's colours always come in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Red is on the outside of the bow.
Sometimes you can see a second, fainter rainbow outside the first one. In that rainbow, the colours run the other way round.

takeaway: Rainbows appear when sun shines through rain with the sun behind you, and their colours always line up in the same order.
materials: A spray bottle of water (an adult uses it)
safetyNotes: Never look directly at the Sun, even when rainbow hunting. Always look away from the sun, towards the rain.
screenFreeExtension: On a sunny day, ask an adult to spray a fine mist of water and look for a tiny rainbow in the spray.
